# Pabbajjā Sutta (Snp 3.1 (PTS Snp 72))
**ID:** Snp 3.1 (PTS Snp 72)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Pabbajjā Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp3.1

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Pabbajjā Sutta* is the opening discourse of the Mahāvagga, the third section of the *Suttanipāta* [Humphreys 1956; Anderson and Smith 1913; Jennings 1948]. Composed in verse (beginning at verse 405 in the PTS edition), the sutta relates the story of the young Bodhisatta's renunciation of household life—which he sees as confined and dusty, in contrast to the open air of going forth (*abbhokāso ca pabbajjā*)—and his subsequent alms round in Rājagaha (Giribbaja), the capital of Magadha [Anderson and Smith 1913; Jennings 1948; SuttaCentral]. King Bimbisāra, watching from his terrace, is struck by the recluse's peaceful demeanour and sends royal messengers to follow him to his dwelling on Mount Paṇḍava [Adikaram 1946; Gjellerup 1999; Jennings 1948]. The king visits the Bodhisatta and offers him wealth and a place in his court, but the Bodhisatta declines, explaining the motives of his spiritual quest [Burlingame 1921; Jennings 1948; SuttaCentral].
Scholars classify the work as an archaic narrative ballad, composed predominantly in the third person [Katre 1931; Lamotte 1988]. It is intimately related to the succeeding *Padhāna Sutta* (Snp 3.2), and early ballad analysis suggests both texts originally formed a single continuous narrative of renunciation and striving before being divided by canonical compilers [Katre 1931; Pande 1974]. While the episode served as a foundational source for later canonical and post-canonical biographies—such as the Jātaka-nidāna and the Dhammapada commentary [Burlingame 1921]—commentators note that this early encounter between Bimbisāra and the pre-enlightenment Bodhisatta is absent from the first four Nikāyas and may represent an idealized or poetic composition [Jennings 1948; Pande 1974].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral include sections from the *Mahāvastu* (Mvu 52, Gotama's Early Wanderings), the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya *Pabbajjā Khandhaka*, and the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Saṅghabhedavastu* [SuttaCentral], a correspondence also corroborated by Pande [Pande 1974]. DharmaNexus concurs with these parallels, identifying 46 automatic alignments with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* as well as extensive Tibetan alignments in the *Abhiniṣkramaṇa-sūtra* (D0301) and the *Vinayavastu* (D0001-4) [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus records 13 matching passages shared with the commentary, the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
